title: Powers of Ten and Place Value

steps.body: Every place value IS a power of ten: the thousands place is 10³, the ones place is 10⁰, the tenths place is 10⁻¹, the hundredths place is 10⁻². Writing 4,000 as 4 × 10³ just names which place value the 4 sits in.

widget.prompt: Which power of ten is the HUNDREDTHS place?

choices.label: 10⁻²
choices.feedback: Right — hundredths is two steps past the decimal point: 10⁻².

choices.label: 10²
choices.feedback: That's the HUNDREDS place (a whole number place), not hundredths.

choices.label: 10⁻¹
choices.feedback: That's the TENTHS place, one step, not two.

choices.label: 10⁰
choices.feedback: That's the ones place — hundredths is two steps further right.

widget.successFeedback: Right — hundredths is two steps past the decimal point: 10⁻².
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect at least 1 base-ten stage before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the aligned place-value model and the inspected stages.

steps.body: This lets us write any number as a digit times a power of ten. 4,000 = 4 × 10³ (the 4 is in the thousands place). 0.007 = 7 × 10⁻³ (the 7 is in the thousandths place) — this idea is exactly what scientific notation is built on.
Write a number using a power of ten.
explanationVariants: 4,000 has its nonzero digit in the thousands place, which is 10³, so 4,000 = 4 × 10³.
Counting place values from the ones place: thousands is three steps left, 10³.

widget.prompt: 4,000 written as a digit times a power of ten is:

choices.label: 4 × 10³
choices.feedback: Right — 4 sits in the thousands place, 10³.

choices.label: 4 × 10⁴
choices.feedback: That would be 40,000 — one power too many.

choices.label: 4 × 10⁻³
choices.feedback: The negative exponent is for numbers SMALLER than 1 — 4,000 is a whole number.

choices.label: 40 × 10²
choices.feedback: That's not in standard digit-times-power form — the digit part should be a single digit: 4 × 10³.

widget.successFeedback: Right — 4 sits in the thousands place, 10³.
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect at least 2 base-ten stages before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the aligned place-value model and the inspected stages.

steps.body: Write a small decimal using a power of ten.

widget.prompt: 0.007 written as a digit times a power of ten is:

choices.label: 7 × 10⁻³
choices.feedback: Right — 7 sits in the thousandths place, 10⁻³.

choices.label: 7 × 10³
choices.feedback: That's a POSITIVE exponent, which gives a big number (7,000), not a small decimal.

choices.label: 7 × 10⁻²
choices.feedback: That would be 0.07 — one place too big.

choices.label: 0.7 × 10⁻²
choices.feedback: That's not standard digit-times-power form — the digit part should be a single nonzero digit: 7 × 10⁻³.

widget.successFeedback: Right — 7 sits in the thousandths place, 10⁻³.
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect at least 2 base-ten stages before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the aligned place-value model and the inspected stages.

steps.body: Every place value is a power of ten — this is the foundation of scientific notation.
takeaways: Any number can be written as a digit times a power of ten.
This 'digit × power of ten' form is exactly what scientific notation uses.

concept.body: Every place value is a power of ten: thousands=10³, ones=10⁰, tenths=10⁻¹, hundredths=10⁻². A number can be written as a digit times its place value's power of ten.

numericErrors.feedback: That treats the exponent as a multiplier of 3 rather than a place value — 3×10²=3×100=300.
